summary.title: Entity–attribute–value model - Wikipedia
summary.one_liner: EAV is a database design that stores sparse, ad-hoc data as three-column (entity, attribute, value) rows instead of one column per property, and what it costs in metadata and validation.
keywords: when to use eav instead of columns
takeaways: EAV stores each fact as an entity-attribute-value row, which suits sparse data with many attribute types that change over time.
Values are typically split into separate tables by data type, because storing everything as strings makes indexing and validation hard.
An EAV system depends on a large metadata subschema (attribute definitions, validation, presentation) that is hard to maintain and must be carefully documented.
Use standard relational columns for dense, stable attributes; EAV is for hybrid cases where only a small part of the data is sparse.
Pivoting EAV rows into columns is needed before most off-the-shelf analysis tools can use the data.
summary.summary: The Wikipedia article describes the entity–attribute–value (EAV) model, a data design for space-efficient storage of sparse or ad-hoc property values, with examples from clinical records and supermarket receipts. It contrasts EAV with row modeling, explains why values are split into per-type tables, and covers the history from early medical record systems (1970s) to later relational and JSON-based approaches. It also discusses EAV/CR (classes and relationships), the heavy metadata requirements, and the maintainability trade-offs. The page is reference-style with a few citations marked as needed.
